title: Chemical kinetics and the reversible-reaction model
summary: How fast: reaction rates and rate laws from experiment, integrated rate laws and half-lives, mechanisms tested against rate laws (rate-determining step, pre-equilibrium, steady state), the temperature dependence of rate constants, and the kinetic view of equilibrium through an original virtual model of a reversible first-order reaction A ⇌ B at constant volume, with its conservation law, relaxation and the observations that distinguish equilibrium from no reaction.

objectives.description: Define reaction rate with stoichiometric coefficients, determine orders and the rate constant from initial-rate data, and give the units of k.
Derive and use the integrated first- and second-order rate laws and half-lives, and identify order from linear plots.

Derive the rate law predicted by a mechanism using the rate-determining-step, pre-equilibrium and steady-state approximations, compare it with experiment and say what experiment would distinguish the limits.
Use the Arrhenius equation and reaction coordinate diagrams to relate rate constants, activation energy and temperature, and explain what a catalyst changes.

For the reversible first-order model A ⇌ B at constant volume, derive the conservation law and the solution, identify the equilibrium composition, relaxation time and K = k_f/k_r, analyse parameter changes and name observations that distinguish dynamic equilibrium from no reaction, stating all model assumptions.

preparation.description: OpenStax 12.1 Chemical Reaction Rates and 12.3 Rate Laws: rate definitions, relative rates, method of initial rates, units of k (Examples 12.1–12.5).
Lecture 30 notes pages 3–6: rate laws come from experiment, reaction order, the integrated first-order law by separation of variables, the first-order half-life.
OpenStax 12.4 Integrated Rate Laws: first-, second- and zero-order laws, half-lives, graphical determination of order (Examples 12.6–12.12).

OpenStax 12.6 Reaction Mechanisms (elementary steps, molecularity, rate laws from mechanisms; Example 12.14) with lecture 32 notes pages 1–3 for the steady-state approximation and the rate-determining step.
Lecture 32 notes page 2: the steady-state approximation and the rate-determining step.
Lecture 31 notes page 4: at equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal, so K = k1/k−1 for elementary steps.
OpenStax 12.5 Collision Theory (activation energy, Arrhenius equation; Example 12.13) and 12.7 Catalysis, with lecture 33 notes pages 1–2 and 4.

activities.title: Lectures 30–33 and OpenStax chapter 12: rates, mechanisms, temperature
activities.instructions: Read the lesson with the lecture notes open. Every time a rate law appears, write next to it whether it came from experiment or from a proposed mechanism. Redo the lesson's worked rate-law and half-life examples before reading on, and derive the pre-equilibrium result for the notes' NO + O2 mechanism yourself before reading the notes' derivation.

activities.title: Optional: the recorded kinetics lectures
activities.instructions: The OCW pages for lectures 30–33 embed the videos (about 50 minutes each). Optional; not individually verified by Corniversity, so start from the lecture pages.

activities.title: Tutorial: rate laws from data and from mechanisms
activities.instructions: Attempt exercises 1 and 2 before asking for hints. In exercise 1 show the ratio of rates you used for each order and give the units of k. In exercise 2 define 'rate' explicitly before writing any rate expression, so the factor of 2 is handled consciously.

activities.title: Virtual laboratory: reversible first-order reaction A ⇌ B
activities.instructions: A virtual model activity, not a laboratory procedure: the system is a stated pair of differential equations, and the only apparatus is the simulator. Derive first (exercise 3, parts 1–2), then run the model with the given rate constants, compare its curves with your formula, change one rate constant at a time, and write the report. Label the model's outputs as model outputs, never as measurements of a real reaction.

activities.title: Explain: what a catalyst does and does not do
activities.instructions: Without the notes, write in the notebook what a catalyst changes (the mechanism and activation energy, hence both rate constants) and what it leaves unchanged (ΔG°, K, the equilibrium composition), with a reaction coordinate sketch. Compare with lecture 33 page 4 and OpenStax 12.7.

activities.title: Retrieval: the unit's relations
activities.instructions: From memory: the rate expression with coefficients; rate = k[A]^m[B]^n and how m is found; ln[A]t = ln[A]0 − kt and t½ = ln 2/k; 1/[A]t = 1/[A]0 + kt; the steady-state condition; K = k_f/k_r for an elementary step; the Arrhenius equation and its two-temperature form.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 3 (the virtual model report) accepted: conservation law and solution derived, equilibrium composition, K and relaxation time computed and compared with the simulator, the two parameter-doubling cases analysed correctly, two distinguishing observations named with the model's predictions, and the assumptions listed; plus exercise 1 accepted with the rate law, k with units and the half-life.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The rate law can be read from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Only for an elementary step. For an overall reaction the orders are experimental quantities and may be fractional, zero or negative (lecture 30, page 3).

commonMisconceptions.claim: At equilibrium the reaction has stopped.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Both directions continue at equal rates; the net rate is zero. Perturbing the composition, labelling a reactant or changing the temperature reveals the ongoing exchange, which a non-reacting mixture would not show (lecture 31, page 4; OpenStax 13.1).

commonMisconceptions.claim: Doubling a rate constant doubles the equilibrium yield.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Doubling k_f alone changes K = k_f/k_r and the equilibrium composition and shortens the relaxation time; doubling both k_f and k_r leaves K and the composition unchanged and only shortens the relaxation time. Where a reaction ends and how fast it gets there are separate questions.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A catalyst increases the equilibrium amount of product.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of forward and reverse steps alike, so both rate constants rise by the same factor and K is unchanged; only the time to reach equilibrium falls (lecture 33, page 4; OpenStax 12.7).

checks.name: mathematical-review
checks.evidence: Content agent re-derived: initial-rate data give second order in NO, first in Cl2, k = 1.8e-4/(0.10² × 0.10) = 0.18 M⁻² s⁻¹; k = 2.50e-3 s⁻¹ gives t½ = 277 s and t(10%) = ln 10/k = 921 s. Mechanism: pre-equilibrium gives ½ d[NOCl]/dt = k2(k1/k−1)[NO]²[Cl2]; steady state gives k1k2[NO]²[Cl2]/(k−1 + k2[NO]) with the two limits. Reversible model: d([A]+[B])/dt = 0; [A](t) = A_eq + (A_0 − A_eq)e^{−(kf+kr)t}; A_eq = kr C0/(kf + kr) = 0.250 M, B_eq = 0.750 M, K = 3.00, τ = 2.50 min, t½ = 1.733 min, A(5 min) = 0.3515 M; kf doubled: A_eq = 0.143 M, K = 6, τ = 1.43 min; both doubled: A_eq = 0.250 M, K = 3, τ = 1.25 min. Lesson examples use different numbers (k = 0.0150 s⁻¹, t½ = 46.2 s; N2O5 rate relations).

checks.name: answer-leakage
checks.evidence: The lesson states the model's equations and the general principle that forward and reverse rates are equal at equilibrium but does not give the solution, the equilibrium values or the perturbation analysis; the lesson's mechanism example is the notes' NO + O2 system, not the exercise's NO + Cl2. Reference values only in instructor/.

checks.name: workload-sanity
checks.evidence: 135 minutes of preparation, 90 of reading, 90 of tutorial, 90 of virtual laboratory, 15 + 15 of explanation and revision ≈ 7.3 hours, plus an optional 100 minutes of recorded lectures; one teaching week, with the laboratory report allowed to spill into the following week.
